newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia signs anti-drug accord with wary U.S..
newsitem.headline: Colombia signs anti-drug accord with wary U.S..

text.p: Colombia signed an anti-drug shipping agreement with Washington on Thursday, a day after beefing up its penalties for drug trafficking in a bid to stave off threatened U.S. economic sanctions.

The maritime ship-boarding agreement, which clears the way for U.S. Coast Guard searches aboard Colombian vessels outside the country's 12-mile limit, is something the United States had sought to negotiate for the last six years.

It is highly controversial, since politicians have bridled for years against the idea of U.S. vessels policing Colombians on the high seas, and Venezuela is the only other country on the Latin American mainland that has such an agreement.

In practice, however, it merely formalised something the United States has been doing for years with the quiet consent of Colombian authorities. U.S. authorities have detained at least 30 Colombian ships on drug-smuggling charges since 1990.

Colombia is under intense U.S. pressure to step up its war against billionaire cocaine merchants and the maritime accord was included on a long list of demands Washington made last year, when it warned that Colombia faced a suspension of trade benefits or other sanctions unless its performance improved.

Other demands included the passage of an asset forfeiture law to take wealth away from convicted drug lords, which was approved by Congress late last year, and stiffer penalities for trafficking, which were passed by both houses of Congress in back-to-back sessions on Tuesday and Wednesday.

U.S. officials were unhappy last month when a Colombian judge handed down extremely lenient prison terms for brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the top leaders of the powerful Cali drug cartel who once cornered up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade. The sentences could see them walk free in as little as five years.
The legislation approved this week increases the maximum penalty for trafficking from 24 to 60 years and cracks down on Colombia's controversial plea-bargaining system.

The sentencing law is not retroactive so the brothers look safe for now. But Justice Minister Carlos Medellin has said the government will move to lift Colombia's 5-year-old ban on extradition next month, which could clear the way for them to be sent to the United States where they face the likelihood of multiple life terms in a maximum security prison.

Officials led by President Ernesto Samper, who said on Wednesday that "Colombians don't need someone to pressure us to be honest," have bent over backwards to deny that they were cracking down on drugs because Washington told them to do so.

But U.S. officials scoff at claims that Samper, or almost anyone else in his scandal-plagued government, is acting of their own free will. U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard last week called Samper "a truly corrupt president" who had failed "to confront fully the drug interests that contributed millions of dollars" to his 1994 election.

Gelbard said it was only because Washington "decertified" Colombia as an ally in the drug war last year and because of "international pressure and the threat of economic sanctions," that progress was finally being made on the legislative front.

U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette said the maritime accord and the law increasing jail terms for traffickers would be taken into account when President Bill Clinton announces next Thursday whether Colombia should remain on a list of virtual pariah states including Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria that have failed to cooperate in the anti-drug fight.

Decertification for a second consecutive year could prompt stringent economic sanctions that Clinton stopped short of imposing last year. Frechette told foreign journalists the Clinton administration would also take into account a 30 percent increase in Colombia's coca production last year and the fact that drugs lords "are going like gangbusters."
